headline: How Karpathy's LLM Wiki Turns Raw Sources Into a Living Knowledge Base
lede: In April 2026, Andrej Karpathy published a short post noting that a growing share of his AI usage had shifted away from code generation toward something quieter: building personal knowledge bases. The post collected more than 16 million views and sent his follow-up GitHub Gist past 5,000 stars within days. The tweet by @himanshustwts annotates that idea with a complete system architecture — from raw document ingest through to Obsidian-rendered markdown and Marp-formatted slides.
body:
The diagram maps five functional zones. At the left sits **Data Ingest**: articles, papers, repositories, datasets, and images arrive via a web clipper or an Obsidian extension and land in an immutable `raw/` directory. Nothing written there is touched again — it is the append-only ledger of primary sources.

The LLM Engine is the workhorse in the middle. It compiles raw material into wiki pages, answers research questions on demand, runs *linting* passes (automated consistency checks that flag gaps, duplicates, and missing cross-references), and maintains an index of summaries and backlinks. All of this is orchestrated through a schema file — in Karpathy's published Gist he uses a `CLAUDE.md` — that tells the model what a well-formed wiki page looks like.

The **Knowledge Store** that accumulates is deliberately plain: roughly 100 markdown articles totalling around 400,000 words, held together by backlinks, concept tags, and categories. That plainness is a design choice, not a constraint. It sidesteps *RAG* (retrieval-augmented generation), the more common approach of embedding documents into a vector database so a model can search them at query time. At personal or small-team scale, a tightly maintained markdown corpus is often faster to query, cheaper to run, and far easier to audit than a vector store.

The output layer is richer than typical note-taking systems. Markdown articles flow into Obsidian for navigation; charts are rendered in Matplotlib and filed back into the wiki; presentations are written in *Marp*, a markdown-to-slides format. The loop closes when those artifacts are treated as first-class wiki citizens rather than one-off exports.

The architecture diagram closes with a candid "Future Explorations" column: synthetic data generation from the wiki, and fine-tuning a model on the accumulated corpus. That ambition — using a hand-curated knowledge base as training data for a downstream specialist model — is where the pattern tips from personal productivity tool into something with broader research implications. Whether the quality of LLM-compiled wiki prose is sufficient for fine-tuning is an open question the diagram tactfully labels a vision rather than a roadmap.

concepts.definition: A pattern, described by Andrej Karpathy, in which a language model agent ingests raw sources and continuously maintains a structured markdown knowledge base. Unlike a chatbot that answers questions from scratch, an LLM Wiki accumulates a corpus of human-readable articles that the model can read, update, and cross-reference like a librarian rather than a search engine.

A technique in which documents are converted into numerical vector embeddings and stored in a specialized database. At query time, the system retrieves the most semantically similar chunks and feeds them to a language model as context. RAG scales well to millions of documents but adds infrastructure complexity; the LLM Wiki pattern trades that scalability for simplicity at personal or team scale.

Borrowing the term from software development (where a linter flags code style or logic errors), knowledge linting refers to automated passes in which an LLM checks a wiki for internal inconsistencies, missing data, orphaned articles, and suggested connections. It is the mechanism that prevents a knowledge base from going stale.

An open-source framework that converts markdown files into presentation slides. Because the source is plain text, slides produced in Marp can be version-controlled alongside wiki articles and regenerated automatically — fitting neatly into a markdown-first workflow.

repos.summary: A GitHub Gist published by Andrej Karpathy on April 4, 2026, that describes the LLM Wiki pattern as an 'idea file' meant to be copied and adapted. It specifies the three-layer architecture (raw/, wiki/, schema file), the three core operations (ingest, query, lint), and notes Obsidian as the recommended frontend. Within days of posting it attracted more than 5,000 stars and forks.
